title: menuPass
summary: menuPass is a long-running intrusion set that vendors and, in at least one notable case, a national government have linked to Chinese state-sponsored activity, with the United States Department of Justice announcing charges against individuals described as associated with the group. The cluster is tracked under names including APT10, Stone Panda, Red Apollo, Potassium, and Cicada, and the boundaries of those labels vary between publishers, particularly where the group is described as supporting other operators by granting or reselling access. Public reporting describes targeting of managed service providers and information technology outsourcing firms, defence and aerospace contractors, telecommunications operators, healthcare and pharmaceutical organisations, and government agencies, with victims reported across North America, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The most consequential tradecraft described in reporting is abuse of trusted third-party relationships: managed service providers with legitimate remote administrative access to multiple downstream customers became the entry path to those customers, and in some described waves the group is assessed to have obtained and used service provider credentials and tooling for that purpose. Other reported behaviour includes spearphishing with malicious documents, exploitation of public-facing applications, use of custom backdoors and loaders with modular, extensible designs, abuse of legitimate remote administration software, credential harvesting and use of valid accounts, and long-dwell collection of documents and email before exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Reporting has also described the group selling or providing network access to other state-interest operators, which complicates attribution because the actor that gains entry is not always the actor that exploits it. For defenders, the central lesson is that outsourced administration is a trust boundary: provider credentials, jump hosts, and remote management tooling deserve the same monitoring rigour as internal privileged access.
objectives: Explain how managed service provider trust is abused and what monitoring must exist on provider-connected administration paths.
Design detection for legitimate remote administration tooling used with stolen provider credentials and separate it from routine support activity.
Analyse the risk that network access is sold or handed to another operator and how that affects incident scoping and attribution.
Detect modular backdoor and loader behaviour through host telemetry when static signatures do not apply.
Explain how credential harvesting from administrator workstations enables downstream victim compromise across an outsourcing relationship.
Evaluate contractual and technical controls for third-party access, including just-in-time provisioning and session recording.
Build a threat hunting plan for long-dwell document and email collection using access-pattern anomalies.

beginner.definition: menuPass is a tracking name for a long-running spying group that security companies and at least one government have linked to China. It also appears as APT10, Stone Panda and Red Apollo. The group is best known for entering through outside companies that manage other companies' computers. Reports say it also sold access to other operators.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many organisations let an outside company run their computers and networks. That provider holds powerful keys. If the provider is breached, every customer can be reached through a door that already exists. This makes the supplier a trust boundary, not just a helper. You must log and limit what provider staff can do inside your systems.
howItWorks: The group first breaks into a company that provides technical services to others.
From there they steal the provider's passwords, keys and everyday support tools.
Those details let them log in to customer systems without breaking a single lock.
Once inside, they read mail and documents and copy what interests them.
They use built-in administration tools, so their activity looks like routine support work.
They stay for a long time, and sometimes they hand access to another group.
beginner.example: Think of an office block where one cleaning company has master keys for every floor. The cleaners are trusted, so their van passes the gate without a check. If someone copies those master keys, they can walk into every office in the building. The weakest point is not any single door, but the master key ring.
takeaways: Treat outside support staff as a high-value path into your systems.
Log and limit provider access, and remove it when the work is finished.
Long, quiet collection of mail and documents is the usual goal.
